newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Potholes and pomp, Albania-style.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Potholes and pomp, Albania-style.

text.p: The pomp was in order as the president awarded the outgoing foreign ambassador the country's highest honour, the Order of Mother Teresa. The applause was steady and the speeches -- as appropriate -- a bit too long.

Soon after, in the south, foreign troops approved by the interim government of national unity came to the rescue of some foreign civilians trapped by armed bandits. The visitors had felt threatened by a number of Kalashnikov rifles.

Two events on the same day in the Balkan state of Albania. One in Tirana, involving a controversial outgoing Italian ambassador; the other with a group of international monitors at a restaurant, preparing to oversee forthcoming elections.
Together they illustrate how ex-communist Albania, already Europe's poorest country, has degenerated into a state where the politics and policing are about as potholed as the roads.
The ceremonial connection with Mother Teresa is that she is of Albanian stock. But you would have a hard time finding her Sisters of Mercy in Albania.
Riven by riots and looting since March, the country is heading to what international observers acknowledge will be at least partially flawed elections on June 29.

"The Albanian political class...has lacked the ideas needed for democracy," said prominent writer and poet Dritero Agolli in an interview with daily Gazeta Shqiptare. "A clash of dogmas killed ideas."

Fiddling while Rome burns has become a speciality of Albania's politicians, preferring to secure power and settle old scores over the admittedly tough and thankless task of rebuilding a shattered nation.
ALL OR NOTHING
"Here it's all or nothing," said one Western diplomat: "They take stuff very personally and don't understand how Western institutions work. There's a very high level of personal hatred."
Compromise is not yet an Albanian political concept.
"A disagreement in Albania is seen as a treasonous act because of the intensity of personal connections," said another Westerner, in Albania to observe the polls.
In Albania, if you are a friend, how can you disagree? A now nationwide tradition of blood feuds makes it almost ludicrous to try to agree to differ.

Under the communist rule of Enver Hoxha Albanians had no free will: they got up and presented themselves at the plant or the office, drank coffee, and by their presence or production earned their right to a pension.

Now Albanians, some of their wallets recently fattened beyond imagination in the short time that fraudulent "pyramid" investment schemes were paying out, are unwilling to fall back to another, harder, earth.

"People have got used to drinking Coca-Cola, Fanta; I last drank tapwater in 1990-91," said one Tirana resident. "They do not want to go back to that. I do not, because I think the water system has deteriorated quite a lot since then."

Albania is clearly crumbling, but some individuals appear to have nest-eggs still. What when the pyramid savings, remittances from overseas relatives, or the pickings from looting and banditry run out?
"We have not yet seen the depths of Albania's (economic) decline -- we aren't even close to it," said the diplomat.
For months Albanian workers, students and schoolchildren have been able to use the unrest as an excuse. It was hard to get up and go to the office when there was shooting on the streets.
But now, with the situation calmer, it is hard to get up and work just in case there might be shooting.
As the people, so the politicians.
"It's easy for the politicians to let the gangsters take over," said the diplomat.
"No politician will make the hard decisions. Albanians have no sense of how much in competition they are -- not only in the region, but the world -- for investment."
"As in the United States and other countries, you see in Albania that the bad politics drives out the good," said the Western election observer. "Reasonable people can't find a place in the system."
"It's like children -- badly behaved children," said the diplomat. "People are going to find it harder and harder to survive. There are other countries doing the right thing."
